newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Dry weather in key soy area worries Brazil growers.
newsitem.headline: Dry weather in key soy area worries Brazil growers.

text.p: Farmers in Brazil's key soybean growing region of Rio Grande do Sul began harvesting earlier than usual last week as dry weather caused the beans to mature prematurely, raising concerns about productivity.

"Harvesting began practically 10 days in advance because of the high temperatures in the state during the month of March," said Nideo Barny, agronomist at the Rio Grande do Sul agricultural secretariat.
Rains have been scarce for the last few weeks and some regions have not had any significant showers for 30 days, growers reported.

Early and medium cycle variety soybeans, reacting to the lack of rains, matured earlier than usual while the longer cycle varieties were not receiving enough moisture during the grain formation stage, agronomists said.
"The grains are very small and the weight is low," said Olbaoir Mielke at the Coopermil cooperative in Santa Rosa, where harvesting began a week ahead of schedule.

"The semi-late and late cycle varieties are suffering some damage because of the dryness of the last 25 days," said Barny. "We see a drop in productivity of 10 to 15 percent for this area, which represents more or less a third of the total crop."

In the Ijui region, the damage to the later cycle crop could be even worse, said one agronomist, predicting that productivity would fall below levels seen during the drought-stricken 1995/96 harvest unless it rained soon.
"We started harvesting 10 to 15 days earlier than usual because of the dryness and a series of illnesses that have affected the crop," said Jair Mello, agronomist at the Cotrijui cooperative in Ijui.
Around 30 percent of the total planted area has been harvested with a productivity of 1,900 kilos per hectare, down from a historical average of 2,000 kilos, Mello said.

"But in the 70 percent of planted area that remains to be harvested, productivity will drop between 30 and 40 percent," he warned. "We expect productivity to drop below 1,500 kilos per hectare which was the level we had with the drought last year."
"If we had a quick shower of 30 to 40 mm, it would benefit the uniform maturing of these (later cycle) crops and perhaps prevent some of this expected drop in productivity," he said.

The weather was forecast to remain dry and sunny across the south until Wednesday night, when a cold front was expected to bring weak showers to Rio Grande do Sul and Parana states, said independent meteorologists Somar.
"It is worth pointing out that these rains are still weak and isolated due to the lack of available humidity in the atmosphere," Somar said in a weekly report.
Some beans had already started heading for crushers and the port of Rio Grande but shipping was not due to begin until April 10 to 15, said David Brew, trader at Brasoja.
"We advise people against trying to ship sooner because if you try to ship earlier, all you need is some small delay in the harvest to slow the whole thing down," he said.
Only a small proportion of the crop has been sold in advance, with most growers trying to hold on to their product to obtain the best possible price, traders said.
"At prices below 15 reais ($14.30), 15 to 20 percent maximum of the harvest has already been sold," said Barny.

In the last week, producers in Rio Grande were receiving 17.50 to 18.00 reais per 60-kg bag but these prices were seen falling after the USDA published its highest forecast for U.S. planted area for soybeans since 1980.
Meanwhile, shipping at the key ports of Paranagua and Santos continued at a strong pace with the latter setting a new record daily loading level for soybeans.
The Paranagua port authority reported that in the month to March 30, it loaded 699,667 tonnes soybeans, 501,497 tonnes soymeal and 24,950 tonnes soyoil.
This compared with 274,070 tonnes soybeans, 489,005 tonnes soymeal and 43,228 tonnes soyoil in March of last year.

At Santos, soybean loading peaked at 40,700 tonnes on March 27, compared with a previous high of around 30,000 tonnes, after the port authority Codesp signed a deal with operators on March 24 opening the way for the terminal to function 24 hours a day.
The new system, operating on the basis of six-hour shifts, was to last initially for 90 days, a spokeswoman said.
